title: Colorado OAC Workers' Compensation Decision — WC 5-276-754-001
text:
Office of Administrative Courts
State of Colorado
Workers’ Compensation No. WC 5-276-754-001
Issues
Whether Claimant has proven by a preponderance of the evidence that
⮚
she is entitled to an award of temporary total disability (“TTD”) benefits for the period of
May 14, 2025 through ongoing?
Prior to the hearing, the parties stipulated to an average weekly wage
⮚
(“AWW”) of $1,751.27.
Findings of Fact
1. Claimant sustained an admitted injury arising out of and in the course and
scope of her employment on Jun 13, 2024 when she was involved in a motor vehicle
accident while driving a bus for Employer in Baggs, Wyoming. Claimant sustained
injuries to her neck, back, head and lower right leg.
2. Following Claimant’s injury, Claimant came under the care of Work
Partners Occupational Health. Claimant was initially provided with work restrictions but
was released to return to work without restrictions as of July 24, 2024. Claimant
testified that when she was on work restrictions she was performing office work.
3. After Claimant was released to return to work without restrictions, she
returned to her previous position driving a bus for Employer. Claimant testified that this
position provided her with a split shift where she would operate the bus to drop off
employees at a job site, then do other tasks, before operating the bus again to pick up
the employees from the job site. Claimant testified that while she could perform this
work which involved driving for a few hours before getting a break.
1

4. Claimant testified at hearing that she was furloughed from her
employment effective February 26, 2025. Claimant testified she was instructed to apply
for “job attached” unemployment benefits (which she did apply for and received) as
there was the possibility that Claimant would be rehired by Employer. Claimant testified
she was subsequently terminated on April 22, 2025.
5. Claimant continued to treat with Work Partners and on May 14, 2025,
Claimant was provided with new work restrictions that included no more than three
consecutive hours of driving at a time. Claimant testified at hearing that due to the work
restrictions, Claimant is not able to complete her Class B training for a commercial
drivers’ license.
6. Claimant was provided with new work restrictions on December 9, 2025
that included no more than 3 hours walking per day, 2 hours standing, and 3 hours
sitting per day. Claimant’s restrictions include alternating between standing and sitting.
7. Ms. Brown testified at hearing that she has not returned to work in any
capacity since being laid off by Employer.
8. Employer presented the testimony of Brian Campbell, the Human
Resources (“HR”) Manager for Employer at hearing. Mr. Campbell confirmed Claimant
was injured while working in her position as a crew bus driver. Mr. Campbell noted that
in Claimant’s position with Employer, her work duties included transporting the crews
from the hotel or district office to the work site locations. Mr. Campbell testified that in
addition to these job duties, a crew bus driver may also need to drive the vehicles to
pick up parts for Employer, if necessary. Claimant would also be required to clean the
buses as part of her work duties.
9. Mr. Campbell testified Claimant was released to return to work without
restrictions, but was then furloughed in February 2025. Mr. Campbell testified Claimant
was furloughed as part of a reduction in work force and that while Employer had hoped
to be able to bring people back, Employer was ultimately unable to do so and
approximately 10-12 people were separated from employment with Employer, including
Claimant.
2

10. Mr. Campbell testified that after Claimant was let go, she has not
contacted Employer about being rehired.
11. The ALJ credits Claimant’s testimony at hearing along with the medical
records entered into evidence at hearing and finds that Claimant has established that it
is more probable than not that she is entitled to an award of temporary total disability
benefits beginning May 14, 2025 and continuing until terminated by law. The ALJ
credits the medical records and finds that Claimant has established that as of May 14,
2025 Claimant was provided with work restrictions which constitute a disability for
Claimant that is related to her admitted work injury. The ALJ further credits Claimant’s
testimony at hearing and finds that Claimant was able to work for Employer based on
the split shift she was capable of performing, but has not been able to find employment
within her work restrictions. Therefore, Claimant is entitled to an award of temporary
disability benefits commencing May 14, 2025 and continuing until terminated by law.
12. Claimant testified at hearing that she was involved in a motor vehicle
accident that was not related to her employment with Employer when she was in
Oklahoma on May 30, 2025. Claimant testified that as a result of the May 30, 2025
motor vehicle accident, she had chest wall contusions and injuries to her shins.
Claimant testified that she did not receive work restrictions for the May 30, 2025 motor
vehicle accident. The ALJ finds Claimant’s testimony regarding the May 30, 2025 motor
vehicle accident to be credible and persuasive and finds insufficient evidence presented
at hearing that would establish that the May 30, 2025 motor vehicle accident represents
an intervening event that would termination Claimant’s entitlement to TTD benefits.
Conclusions of Law
A. The purpose of the Workers’ Compensation Act of Colorado, §§ 8-40-101,
et seq., C.R.S. is to assure the quick and efficient delivery of disability and medical
benefits to injured workers at a reasonable cost to employers, without the necessity of
litigation. See § 8-40-102(1), C.R.S. Claimant shoulders the burden of proving
entitlement to benefits by a preponderance of the evidence. See § 8-43-201, C.R.S. A
preponderance of the evidence is that which leads the trier-of-fact, after considering all
3

of the evidence, to find that a fact is more probably true than not. Page v. Clark, 592
P.2d 792 (Colo. 1979). The facts in a workers’ compensation case must be interpreted
neutrally; neither in favor of the rights of the claimant, nor in favor of the rights of
respondents; and a workers’ compensation claim shall be decided on the merits. § 8-43-
201, C.R.S.
B. Assessing weight, credibility, and sufficiency of evidence in Workers'
Compensation proceedings is the exclusive domain of the administrative law judge.
University Park Care Center v. Industrial Claim Appeals Office, 43 P.3d 637 (Colo. App.
2001). Even if other evidence in the record may have supported a contrary inference, it
is for the ALJ to resolve conflicts in the evidence, make credibility determinations, and
draw plausible inferences from the evidence. Id. at 641. When determining credibility,
the fact finder should consider, among other things, the consistency or inconsistency of
the witness's testimony and actions; the reasonableness or unreasonableness
(probability or improbability) of the testimony and actions; the motives of the witness;
whether the testimony has been contradicted; and bias, prejudice, or interest. Prudential
Insurance Co. v. Cline, 57 P.2d 1205 (Colo. 1936); Bodensieck v. Industrial Claim
Appeals Office, 183 P.3d 684 (Colo. App. 2008). The weight and credibility to be
assigned expert testimony is a matter within the discretion of the ALJ. Cordova v.
Industrial Claim Appeals Office, 55 P.3d 186 (Colo. App. 2002). To the extent expert
testimony is subject to conflicting interpretations, the ALJ may resolve the conflict by
crediting part or none of the testimony. Colorado Springs Motors, Ltd. v. Industrial
Commission, 441 P.2d 21 (Colo. 1968).
C. The ALJ's factual findings concern only evidence and inferences found to
be dispositive of the issues involved; the ALJ has not addressed every piece of
evidence or every inference that might lead to conflicting conclusions and has rejected
evidence contrary to the above findings as unpersuasive. Magnetic Eng’g, Inc. v. Indus.
Claim Appeals Office, 5 P.3d 385 (Colo. App. 2000).
D. To prove entitlement to temporary total disability (TTD) benefits, claimant
must prove that the industrial injury caused a disability lasting more than three work
4

shifts, that he left work as a result of the disability, and that the disability resulted in an
actual wage loss. PDM Molding, Inc. v. Stanberg, 898 P.2d 542 (Colo. 1995). Section
8-42-103(1)(a), supra, requires claimant to establish a causal connection between a
work-related injury and a subsequent wage loss in order to obtain TTD benefits. PDM
Molding, Inc. v. Stanberg, supra. The term disability, connotes two elements: (1)
Medical incapacity evidenced by loss or restriction of bodily function; and (2)
Impairment of wage earning capacity as demonstrated by claimant's inability to resume
his prior work. Culver v. Ace Electric, 971 P.2d 641 (Colo. 1999). There is no statutory
requirement that claimant establish physical disability through a medical opinion of an
attending physician; claimant's testimony alone may be sufficient to establish a
temporary disability. Lymburn v. Symbios Logic, 952 P.2d 831 (Colo. App. 1997). The
impairment of earning capacity element of disability may be evidenced by a complete
inability to work, or by restrictions which impair the claimant's ability effectively and
properly to perform his regular employment. Ortiz v. Charles J. Murphy & Co., 964 P.2d
595 (Colo.App. 1998).
E. As found, Claimant has established by a preponderance of the evidence
that she is entitled to an award of TTD commencing May 14, 2025 when she was
provided with work restrictions from her treating physicians that limited her driving ability
to shifts lasting no more than three hours. As found, the testimony of Claimant and
medical records entered into evidence present credible evidence that Claimant is
entitled to an award commencing May 14, 2025 and continuing until terminated by
statute or law.
Order
It is therefore ordered that:
1. Respondents shall pay Claimant TTD benefits based on the stipulated
AWW of $1,751.27 for the period of May 14, 2025 and continuing until terminated by
law or statute.
2. All matters not determined herein are reserved for future determination.
5

NOTE: If you are dissatisfied with the ALJ's order, you may file a Petition to Review the
order with the Denver Office of Administrative Courts, 1525 Sherman St., 4th Floor,
Denver, CO 80203. You must file your Petition to Review within twenty (20) days after
mailing or service of the order, as indicated on the certificate of mailing or service;
otherwise, the ALJ's order will be final. You may file the Petition to Review by mail, as
long as the certificate of mailing attached to your petition shows: (1) That you mailed it
within twenty (20) days after mailing or service of the order of the ALJ; and (2) That you
mailed it to the above address for the Denver Office of Administrative Courts. You may
file your Petition to Review electronically by emailing the Petition to Review to the
following email address: oac-ptr@state.co.us. If the Petition to Review is emailed to the
aforementioned email address, the Petition to Review is deemed filed in Denver
pursuant to OACRP 27 and Section 8-43-301, C.R.S. If the Petition to Review is filed
by email to the proper email address, it does not need to be mailed to the Denver Office
of Administrative Courts. For further information regarding procedures to follow when
filing a Petition to Review, see Rule 27, OACRP. You may access a petition to review
form at: http://www.colorado.gov/dpa/oac/forms-WC.htm.
Dated: June 1, 2026 _/s/ Keith E. Mottram______________
Keith E. Mottram
Administrative Law Judge
6

Office of Administrative Courts
State of Colorado
Workers’ Compensation No. 5-294-708-001
Issues
Whether Claimant proved by a preponderance of the evidence that there existed
➢
a mistake, an error, a change of condition, or fraud warranting a reopening of her
workers’ compensation claim.
If Claimant proved that her claim should be reopened, then whether Claimant
➢
proved by a preponderance of the evidence that she is entitled to disfigurement
benefits.
If Claimant proved that her claim should be reopened, then whether Claimant
➢
proved by a preponderance of the evidence that she is entitled to additional
medical benefits.
If Claimant proved that her claim should be reopened, then whether Claimant
➢
proved by a preponderance of the evidence that she is entitled to permanent total
disability benefits.
If Claimant proved that her claim should be reopened, then whether Claimant
➢
proved by a preponderance of the evidence that the average weekly wage
admitted in the final admission of liability is incorrect.
Findings of Fact
1. Claimant, a 36-year-old female, was an employee whose right foot was injured
while working for Respondent on December 4, 2024.
2. Claimant presented initially to Dr. TwoBears on December 13, 2024, with a
complaint of right foot pain after a fellow employee pushed a roller onto her foot
at work. Claimant reported pain at 8/10. Dr. TwoBears diagnosed Claimant with a

right foot crush injury, ordered ibuprofen, and physical therapy. Dr. TwoBears
additionally ordered light-work duty with accompanying restrictions.
3. On December 18, 2024, Claimant presented to PA-C Skvarca. Claimant
maintained a pain level of 8/10. Claimant reported pain in the right foot-top and
heel; however, ibuprofen was helping. PA-C Skvarca evaluated Claimant’s foot
and noted no symptoms of compartment syndrome, no out-of-proportion pain, no
paresthesia, no pain with range of motion distal to the injury, no pallor
pulselessness, and no paralysis. PA-C Skvarca reviewed Claimant’s X-ray
impressions from her last visit: (1) no acute bony fracture, or joint subluxation or
dislocation; (2) no soft-tissue emphysema, radiodense soft tissue abnormality or
foreign body seen; (3) consider follow-up evaluation with MRI for further
assessment if symptoms persist or worsen.
4. On March 13, 2025, Claimant presented to Dr. Cheesman. Dr. Cheesman
ordered diclofenac sodium and an MRI of the right foot as well as additional
referral for durable medical equipment in addition to prior prescribed orders.
5. On April 10, 2025, Dr. Shinault conducted an MRI of Claimant’s right foot and
had the following impressions: (1) intact lateral ankle ligaments and syndesmotic
ligament complex; (2) intact deltoid ligament complex and spring ligament
complex; (3) intact peroneal, medial flexor, extensor, and Achilles tendons; (4) no
acute or occult fracture, osteochondral lesion along the talar dome, or evidence
of tarsal coalitions; (5) intact tarsal tunnel, sinus tarsi, and plantar fascia, no
significant muscular atrophy, nor signal alterations to suggest denervation-type
injury; and (6) no significant ankle joint effusion or distinct loose bodies in the
synovial space.
6. On April 16, 2025, Claimant presented to podiatrist Dr. Zyzda. Dr. Zyzda
reviewed the MRI, X-ray, and medical history and discussed with Claimant her
treatment options. Claimant reported continued pain and a slight limp. Dr. Zyzda
2

ordered gabapentin 300 mg at bedtime, orthotics, cortisone injection, and referral
for neurological consultation.
7. On April 30, 2025, Claimant presented for follow-up to Dr. Zyzda. Claimant self-
reported being 20% improved. Claimant noted she had an appointment with a
physiatrist the following day. Dr. Zyzda remarked that most of Claimant’s pain
appeared neurogenic given that the MRI and the X-ray were negative.
8. On May 1, 2025, Claimant presented to Dr. Aschberger for physiatrist review.
Claimant reported for the first time she had irritation proximally in the distal
foreleg and paresthesia distally at the toes. Dr. Aschberger increased Claimant’s
gabapentin to 300 mg three times daily for the next “couple of weeks.” Dr.
Aschberger noted possible plantar fasciitis in addition to the initial crush injury
diagnosis. Dr. Aschberger also ordered evaluation of Claimant’s foot to rule out
complex regional pain syndrome. He wrote in his report that he recommended
electrodiagnostic testing “to rule out neural compromise.” On the same day,
Claimant presented to Dr. Zyzda for fitting and ordered her back in three weeks
for orthotic fitting and neurological review.
9. On May 8, 2025, Claimant presented to Dr. Cheesman for follow-up occupational
care. Dr. Cheesman noted Claimant was “hyper emotional” and “extremely
charge[d]” resulting in a request for a chaperone for Claimant as Claimant was
“inconsolable.” Dr. Cheesman noted that he was unable to get coherent
information from Claimant as Claimant was attempting to explain while “crying
hysterically” and her attempts were “very convoluted.” Claimant expressed she
did not feel comfortable or safe going to the other Concentra clinic. Dr.
Cheesman noted that Claimant felt that she was slighted in some manner.
10. On May 23, 2025, Claimant presented to Dr. Muthiah Nachiappan at UC Health
for a Bone/Joint 3 Phase bone scan. Dr. Nachiappan’s impression was negative,
noting: (1) no significant abnormality or asymmetry in blood flow (radionuclide
3

angiography); (2) no significant abnormality or asymmetry in blood pool (soft
tissue); and (3) expected distribution of radiotracer on delayed phase imaging
(skeletal.)
11. On May 29, 2025, Claimant presented to Dr. Zyzda. Claimant reported orthotics
felt good on her left foot while wearing a surgical shoe for her right foot. Dr.
Zyzda noted Claimant was in no apparent distress and was alert and
cooperative. Claimant reported pain at 7/10, an improvement from earlier in May
when Claimant’s self-reported pain was 8/10.
12. On June 2, 2025, Claimant presented to UC Health for an EMG performed by Dr.
Dianna Quan. Dr. Quan’s findings noted, “this was [a] normal study. There was
no electrophysiologic evidence of a generalized polyneuropathy or focal
entrapment neuropathy affecting the symptomatic right lower limb at this time.”
13. On June 6, 2025, Claimant presented to Dr. Cheesman. Dr. Cheesman noted
that the EMG did not show any evidence of lower extremity involvement. Dr.
Cheesman noted Claimant appeared more comfortable with her orthotics and
they neither caused her pain nor discomfort in the right foot.
14. On June 11, 2025, Claimant presented to Dr. Zyzda for podiatrist follow-up.
Claimant noted she performed a three-phase bone scan and EMG at UC Health.
Claimant reported that the orthotics were not making much of a difference. On
evaluation, Dr. Zyzda noted, “She essentially has hypersensitivity and pain
everywhere I touch on the foot and ankle.” Dr. Zyzda noted there appeared only
to be neurogenic pain and discharged Claimant as she was at maximum medical
improvement (“MMI”) orthopedically with orders to follow up with Dr. Aschberger.
15. On June 18, 2025, Claimant presented to Dr. Aschberger. Dr. Aschberger noted
that Claimant was “quite angry” and reported numerous issues. First, Claimant
stated that the prescription for her gabapentin has been sent in incorrectly with
4

verification that two refills had been provided to Claimant. Claimant reported she
did not refill the medications. Dr. Aschberger verified the prescriptions were
correctly sent in and filled. Second, Claimant reported obtaining a three-phase
bone scan at UC Health. Dr. Aschberger noted this referral did not originate from
their office. Next, Dr. Aschberger reviewed Claimant’s three-phase bone scan
and noted it was negative for any findings by both him and UC Health. Dr.
Aschberger wrote, “I do not believe it is possible to establish a further working
relationship with [Claimant.]” Dr. Aschberger further wrote, “[Claimant] is
skeptical regarding testing results as performed, although this was performed at
UC Health, outside our facilities, and she has expressed skepticism regarding
recommendations.” Dr. Aschberger found Claimant’s symptoms were negative
for CRPS and the current examination, including three-phase bone scan by UC
Health. Dr. Aschberger maintained Gabapentin orders and opined with Dr.
Cheesman that a psychological assessment is warranted “to help determine
whether therapeutic relationship is possible and the appropriate approach.”
Claimant walked out of the appointment without scheduling any further
evaluations.
16. On July 9, 2025, Claimant presented to Dr. Cheesman for follow-up. Dr.
Cheesman noted Claimant appeared with a workup for CRPS inconsistent with
CRPS given the 3D bone scan and EMG. Dr. Cheesman observed that Claimant
was aggressively emotional and that he was unable to understand her at times
due to the outbursts of tears, flight of speech, and convoluted nature of speech.
Dr. Cheesman offered Claimant an interpreter, which Claimant declined.
Claimant stated she cannot function with activities of daily living and believes her
coworkers are upset with her due to her medication use and naps throughout the
day. Dr. Cheesman noted Dr. Aschberger recommended pain psychology;
however, there was an unclear source for the pain.
17. On August 6, 2025, Claimant presented to Dr. Cheesman. Dr. Cheesman did not
have a source for Claimant’s significant debilitation. Claimant requested a pill that
5

would make her feel better, noting that she did not want to take gabapentin any
longer due to how it made her sleepy. Dr. Cheesman advised Claimant that all
medications have some form of side effect and there was not a singular drug he
could prescribe that would fully alleviate Claimant’s symptomology. Dr.
Cheesman placed Claimant at MMI with no impairment rating.
18. On September 4, 2025, Claimant presented to Dr. Cheesman. Dr. Cheesman
documented that the referral for a second opinion to another physiatrist was
declined by the other physiatrist. Claimant presented somberly and refused to
communicate with Dr. Cheesman. Claimant requested an Ewe interpreter from
Ghana. Dr. Cheesman noted they were unable to get an interpreter with her
dialect that day as the phone interpreters spoke with a Togo dialect. Claimant
reported she did not wish to proceed without an interpreter present. Dr.
Cheesman noted Claimant has been offered an interpreter at prior appointments
and Claimant was only now raising the need for an interpreter. Dr. Cheesman
noted Claimant was at MMI from August 6, 2025, visit.
19. On September 30, 2025, Claimant presented to Dr. Cheesman. Dr. Cheesman
secured an interpreter that permitted Claimant to speak in a mixture of English
and Ewe. Dr. Cheesman noted that Claimant was okay with proceeding forward
with the mixed interpretations. Dr. Cheesman discussed the lack of objective
findings and the lack of any localization for the pain she reports with multiple
diagnostics. Claimant reported that someone had told her that there were
abnormalities with her nerves; however, Dr. Cheesman observed that all nerve
diagnostics were negative. Dr. Cheesman noted Claimant remained at MMI. Dr.
Cheesman had released Claimant to full duty on that date without restrictions
and without any permanent impairment. Dr. Cheesman noted that Claimant
reached MMI on August 06, 2025.
20. On October 2, 2025, Respondents filed its Final Admission of Liability
documenting medical benefits paid as $7,043.76, TTD totaling $2,044.96, TPD
6

totaling $4,003.69, no impairment rating or PPD, and no maintenance medical
care. Respondents asserted an overpayment of $1,666.67.
21. The Court notes an absence of credible evidence in the record that Claimant
challenged the October 2, 2025 FAL within thirty days by requesting a hearing or
a DIME. The Court therefore finds that the claim closed on the October 2, 2025
FAL.
22. Dr. Leland at UC Health noted in his report on August 28, 2025:
“I saw and evaluated the patient. I discussed the case with Dr. Rakowski
and agree with the findings [and] plan as documented. Patient does not
have any evidence of any structural abnormalities in her right foot
following her crush injury. That being said, she does have some nerve
hypersensitivity and concern over development of complex regional pain
syndrome. It was recommended that a pain management referral be
obtained. Additionally, to ensure that there is no evidence of any structural
damage, an MRI was ordered.”
23. Dr. Leland did not make any note of Claimant’s prior medical imaging.
24. On October 19, 2025, Claimant presented for an MRI of her right foot. Dr.
Leland’s impression was negative for any evidence of structural abnormalities.
He recommended that Claimant progress in her activity as tolerated. Dr. Leland
specifically wrote, “In light of the fact that her symptoms have resolved and her
MRI shows no evidence of any structural abnormalities, continued nonoperative
treatment course is recommended.” Dr. Leland did not recommend any curative
medical treatment.
25. However, even Dr. Leland noted Claimant was negative for any indicators and
discharged Claimant on October 23, 2025. Dr. Leland also documented that
7

Claimant’s self-reported symptoms had resolved and that the dorsal foot swelling
was resolving. Dr. Leland’s orders included follow-up as needed with activity to
progress as she could tolerate.
26. Claimant testified at hearing on her own behalf.
27. Claimant testified that she had accepted a twelve-week position with Employer
and had signed on to begin working full time at a rate of $20.77 per hour prior to
her injury.
28. Claimant testified that after her injury, she went to Concentra for tetanus shots
and was experiencing leg pain. She testified that she subsequently treated with
different doctors and was placed on temporary restrictions. According to
Claimant, her employer threatened to fire her while she was subject to those
restrictions.
29. Claimant testified that her podiatrist, Dr. Zyzda, diagnosed her with plantar
fasciitis and prescribed gabapentin to help her sleep. Claimant further testified
that physical therapists noted she had achieved only 25% of her pre-injury
capacity by February 2025.
30. Claimant testified that the MRI she underwent examined only her ankle, not her
foot, and that she was unable to keep her leg straight during the MRI.
31. Claimant testified that she was required to use an interpreter during the
September 30 medical examination.
32. Claimant testified that, at the time she was placed at maximum medical
improvement (MMI), she continued to have restrictions imposed by Dr.
Cheesman. Claimant testified that the existence of those restrictions was not
documented in Dr. Cheesman's report, which she contended evidenced fraud or
8

error. Based on this contention, Claimant testified that her claim should not have
been closed.
33. Claimant testified that she decided in December to seek reopening of her claim
because her condition was “still ongoing.” She further testified that the claim
should not have been closed while referrals remained pending, including referrals
to a spine specialist and a psychiatrist at UC Health. Additionally, she testified
that her prior attorney did not communicate with her regarding the closure of her
claim, resulting in her missing the deadline to object to the final admission of
liability.
34. Claimant testified regarding the May 1, 2025 report of Dr. Aschberger.
Specifically, she testified that Dr. Aschberger's recommendation for
electrodiagnostic testing “to rule out neural compromise” demonstrated that he
was predisposed to find no neural compromise. Claimant's testimony suggested
that she believed Dr. Aschberger had prejudged her condition.
35. Claimant testified that she later sought treatment in an emergency room after the
claim was closed and that she was homeless at that time.
36. With respect to disfigurement, Claimant testified that the right corner of her foot
had edema and that her toes were not in the proper position.
37. The Court finds Claimant’s testimony only partially credible. The Court does not
doubt that Claimant sustained a compensable right-foot injury on December 13,
2024, and experienced pain and discomfort thereafter. However, the severity and
persistence of the symptoms and limitations described at hearing are not fully
supported by the greater weight of the evidence. Throughout the course of
treatment, multiple objective diagnostic studies—including X-rays, an MRI, a
three-phase bone scan, and EMG testing—failed to identify a structural,
neurological, or other objective basis for the degree of impairment alleged by
9

Claimant. Treating providers repeatedly documented normal or negative findings,
ruled out complex regional pain syndrome, and ultimately placed Claimant at
maximum medical improvement without permanent impairment. The Court
further notes that several providers documented difficulties in obtaining coherent
information from Claimant, observed significant emotional responses
disproportionate to examination findings, and recorded Claimant’s skepticism
regarding negative diagnostic results and medical recommendations. Claimant’s
hearing testimony was also inconsistent with portions of the medical record,
including her assertion that the MRI did not evaluate her foot and her contention
that undisclosed restrictions remained in place at the time of MMI despite the
contemporaneous medical records reflecting otherwise. While the Court credits
Claimant’s subjective reports of ongoing pain and acknowledges her sincere
belief that she remained symptomatic, the Court affords greater weight to the
objective medical evidence and the opinions of the treating physicians.
Accordingly, the Court finds that Claimant’s testimony is credible only to the
extent it establishes the occurrence of the work injury and some resulting
symptoms, but not to the extent it alleges ongoing disabling impairment,
entitlement to additional benefits, or error in the closure of the claim.
38. The Court finds that Claimant has not proved by a preponderance of the
evidence that there existed a change of condition warranting reopening.
Following closure of the claim on October 2, 2025, the records documented
continued complaints of pain but did not show any worsening of Claimant’s
condition. To the contrary, the post-closure medical evidence is consistent with
the findings that existed at the time of maximum medical improvement. Dr.
Leland’s evaluation and subsequent MRI failed to identify any structural
abnormality of the right foot and did not result in any recommendation for curative
treatment. Rather, Dr. Leland documented that Claimant’s symptoms had
resolved, noted improvement in the previously reported swelling, recommended
only progression of activity as tolerated, and discharged Claimant from care on
an as-needed basis. The Court further finds that Claimant’s disagreement with
10

the opinions of the authorized treating physicians, her belief that additional
referrals should have been pursued, and her continued subjective complaints of
pain are insufficient to lead the Court to a contrary finding.
39. The Court finds that Claimant has not proved by a preponderance of the
evidence that there existed a mistake or error warranting reopening in this case.
The claim in this matter was closed not as the result of any factual or legal
mistake, but as the result of Respondents’ October 2, 2025 Final Admission of
Liability becoming final after Claimant failed to timely contest it within thirty days.
The Court finds that Respondents filed a Final Admission of Liability on October
2, 2025, based upon the opinions of the authorized treating physicians that
Claimant had reached maximum medical improvement without permanent
impairment and without the need for additional curative treatment. Those
opinions were supported by extensive diagnostic testing, including X-rays, MRI
imaging, a three-phase bone scan, and EMG studies, all of which were
essentially negative for objective findings explaining the level of impairment
alleged by Claimant. Although Claimant contends that the claim should not have
closed because additional referrals remained pending, because she disagreed
with the opinions of the treating physicians, because she believes the MRI was
inadequate, and because she did not timely challenge the Final Admission of
Liability due to a lack of communication with her former attorney, those
circumstances do not establish a mistake or error underlying the closure of the
claim which would warrant reopening the claim in the Court’s view. The Court
further finds no persuasive evidence that Dr. Cheesman incorrectly placed
Claimant at maximum medical improvement, failed to document material
restrictions that actually existed, or otherwise made a mistake that would justify
reopening. At most, the evidence demonstrates Claimant's disagreement with the
medical conclusions reached by the authorized providers and her dissatisfaction
with the closure of the claim.
11

40. The Court finds that Claimant has not proved by a preponderance of the
evidence that there exists fraud in this case warranting a reopening. Although
Claimant suggested that fraud occurred because Dr. Cheesman allegedly failed
to document continuing work restrictions at the time he placed her at maximum
medical improvement, the record contains no evidence persuasively supporting
that allegation. The Court finds no credible evidence that any physician,
employer, insurer, or other participant in the claim knowingly misrepresented
material facts, concealed relevant information, falsified medical records, or
otherwise engaged in deceptive conduct. Rather, the evidence demonstrates that
Claimant received extensive medical evaluation and diagnostic testing from
multiple providers over an extended period of time. The conclusions reached by
those providers were generally consistent in finding an absence of objective
abnormalities sufficient to support ongoing impairment, permanent restrictions, or
additional curative treatment. Claimant’s dissatisfaction with those conclusions
and her belief that the providers were mistaken, biased, or should have pursued
additional testing do not establish fraud. Nor does the fact that Claimant
disagrees with the determination that she reached maximum medical
improvement constitute evidence of fraudulent conduct.
Conclusions of Law
Generally
A. The purpose of the Workers’ Compensation Act of Colorado, §§ 8-40-101, et
seq., C.R.S., is to assure the quick and efficient delivery of disability and medical
benefits to injured workers at a reasonable cost to employers, without the
necessity of litigation. See § 8-40-102(1), C.R.S. Claimant shoulders the burden
of proving entitlement to benefits by a preponderance of the evidence. See § 8-
43-201, C.R.S. A preponderance of the evidence is that which leads the trier-of-
fact, after considering all of the evidence, to find that a fact is more probably true
than not. Page v. Clark, 592 P.2d 792 (Colo. 1979). The facts in a workers’
compensation case must be interpreted neutrally; neither in favor of the rights of
12

the claimant, nor in favor of the rights of respondents; and a workers’
compensation claim shall be decided on the merits. § 8-43-201, C.R.S.
B. Assessing weight, credibility, and sufficiency of evidence in Workers'
Compensation proceeding is the exclusive domain of the administrative law judge.
University Park Care Center v. Industrial Claim Appeals Office, 43 P.3d 637 (Colo.
App. 2001). Even if other evidence in the record may have supported a contrary
inference, it is for the ALJ to resolve conflicts in the evidence, make credibility
determinations, and draw plausible inferences from the evidence. Id. at 641. When
determining credibility, the fact finder should consider, among other things, the
consistency or inconsistency of the witness's testimony and actions; the
reasonableness or unreasonableness (probability or improbability) of the
testimony and actions; the motives of the witness; whether the testimony has been
contradicted; and bias, prejudice, or interest. Prudential Insurance Co. v. Cline, 57
P.2d 1205 (Colo. 1936); Bodensieck v. Industrial Claim Appeals Office, 183 P.3d
684 (Colo. App. 2008). The weight and credibility to be assigned expert testimony
is a matter within the discretion of the ALJ. Cordova v. Indus. Claim Appeals Off.,
55 P.3d 186 (Colo. App. 2002). To the extent expert testimony is subject to
conflicting interpretations, the ALJ may resolve the conflict by crediting part or none
of the testimony. Colorado Springs Motors, Ltd. v. Industrial Commission, 441 P.2d
21 (Colo. 1968).
C. The ALJ's factual findings concern only evidence and inferences found to be
dispositive of the issues involved; the ALJ has not addressed every piece of
evidence or every inference that might lead to conflicting conclusions and has
rejected evidence contrary to the above findings as unpersuasive. Magnetic
Engineering, Inc. v. Industrial Claim Appeals Office, 5 P.3d 385 (Colo. App.
2000).
Reopening
D. Once a claim is closed, it may be reopened only on grounds of fraud,
overpayment, error, mistake, or change in condition. Section 8-43-303, C.R.S.
A “change in condition” refers to a “change in the condition of the original
13

compensable injury or to a change in claimant’s physical or mental condition
which can be causally connected to the original compensable injury.” Cordova 55
P.3d 186 at 189; In re Caraveo, W.C. No. 4-358-465 (October 25, 2006).
Reopening is appropriate when the claimant’s degree of permanent disability has
changed since MMI or where the claimant is entitled to additional medical or
temporary disability benefits that are causally connected to the compensable
injury. See Duarte v. Glen Ayr Health Center, W.C. No. 4-521-453 (June 8,
2007).
E. In cases of allegation of a change in condition, the claimant bears the burden of
proof to establish, by a preponderance of the evidence, that the worsening of
their physical or mental condition is causally related to the industrial injury.
Lymburn v. Symbios Logic, 952 P.2d 831 (Colo. App. 1997); Savio House v.
Dennis, 665 P.2d 141 (Colo. App. 1983). However, a change of condition by itself
is not sufficient to justify reopening, and the claimant must also establish that
reopening is appropriate because the claimant’s degree of permanent disability
has changed, or when additional medical or temporary disability benefits are
warranted. Richards v. Indus. Claim Appeals Off., 996 P.2d 756, 758 (Colo. App.
2000).
F. Reopening may be granted based on any mistake of fact that calls into question
the propriety of a prior award. Kehler v. Labor Etc Inc, W.C. No. 5-000-017 at *3
(Jan. 6, 2023). In determining whether a particular mistake of fact or law justifies
reopening, the ALJ may consider whether the mistake could have been avoided
if the party seeking reopening timely exercised procedural or appellate rights
prior to entry of the award. Klosterman v. Indus. Comm’n, 694 P.2d 873 (Colo.
App. 1984); Webster v. Czarnowski Display Service Inc, W.C. No. 5-009-761-014
at *6 (Nov. 16, 2022).
G. The reopening authority granted to ALJs by § 8-43-303 “is permissive, and
whether to reopen a prior award when the statutory criteria have been met is left
to the sound discretion of the ALJ.” Cordova, 55 P.3d at 189.
H. The Court concludes, as found, that Claimant has not proved by a
preponderance of the evidence that reopening is warranted on the bases of
14

mistake, error, change of condition, or fraud. The claim closed by operation of
law when Claimant did not timely contest the October 2, 2025 Final Admission of
Liability through a request for hearing or a DIME. Claimant has not proved the
existence of any factual or legal mistake underlying the closure of the claim that
would warrant reopening, nor has she proved fraud by any physician, employer,
insurer, or other participant. To the contrary, the evidence is that Claimant
received extensive evaluation from multiple providers, including X-rays, MRI
imaging, a three-phase bone scan, and EMG testing, none of which identified
objective findings supporting ongoing disability, permanent impairment, or the
need for additional curative treatment. The Court also notes the post-closure
medical evidence, which is consistent with, rather than contrary to, the opinions
upon which the claim was closed. Although the Court finds that Claimant
sincerely believes she remained symptomatic and disagrees with the conclusions
of the authorized treating physicians, disagreement with medical opinions,
dissatisfaction with claim closure, or the existence of unresolved subjective
complaints does not warrant the Court exercising discretion to reopen Claimant’s
claim. Accordingly, the Court declines to exercise its discretionary authority to
reopen the claim and concludes that Claimant’s request for reopening must be
denied.
Order
It is therefore ordered that:
1. Claimant has not proved by a preponderance of the evidence
that there exists mistake, error, change in condition, or fraud
warranting reopening of her claim.
